analysis.one_liner: Bans agreements requiring workers to pay union fees as a job condition nationwide.
analysis.headline: The National Right-to-Work Act was introduced by Sen. Rand Paul with 31 Republican cosponsors, placed on the Senate calendar, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the parts of federal labor law that let employers and unions sign contracts requiring workers to join the union or pay fees for union representation. About 27 states already ban these agreements; this bill would extend that ban nationwide. Supporters call this protecting workers' choice; critics say it lets workers benefit from union-negotiated contracts without paying for them, draining unions of the money they use to bargain.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers gain leverage: with union fees optional everywhere, unions would collect less and bargain with fewer resources. Individual workers who currently pay agency fees in union shops would keep that money. Anti-union organizations that have pushed right-to-work laws for decades would win a national version of their policy.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the sections of the National Labor Relations Act and the Railway Labor Act that allow employers and unions to require workers to join the union or pay fees as a condition of employment [S2][S3].
Applies to any union agreement entered into or renewed after enactment, so existing contracts would convert to voluntary-dues arrangements when they are renegotiated [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Labor unions lose the dues and fees from workers they represent, which funds contract negotiations, grievances, and organizing. Workers who rely on union bargaining power would face weaker representation; research on right-to-work states generally finds lower union membership and wages where such laws exist.
analysis.who_pays_short: Unions and workers who bargain through them

drawbacks.text: Workers covered by a union contract could stop paying dues while still receiving the negotiated wage and benefits, a free-rider problem that shrinks union budgets over time [S2].

The bill overrides state choices in both directions: the roughly 27 states with right-to-work laws keep their rules, but states that allow union security agreements lose that option entirely [S2][S3].
Because union fee revenue is the main funding for contract enforcement and collective bargaining, weakening it reduces workers' leverage in wage negotiations, not just their payment obligations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives individual workers an unambiguous gain: no one can be compelled to support a union financially. The cost falls on the institutions of collective bargaining. If the free-rider effect plays out as it has in the states, the result is fewer resources for the contracts that set wages for union and non-union workers alike. The tradeoff is real individual choice against the collective machinery that historically raised unionized wages.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar, but the Senate never brought it up for a committee hearing or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Rand Paul introduced the bill on February 27, 2023, with 22 original cosponsors; 31 Republican senators cosponsored in total [S1][S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and placed it on the Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 17) on February 28, 2023 [S5][S3].
No committee referral, hearing, markup, or vote followed; no further action appears in the record for the rest of the 118th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Labor unions and the workers they represent are better off, since a national ban on union security agreements never advanced. Employers and anti-union groups did not get the nationwide policy they sought, but they lost nothing they had.

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Right-to-Work Act and put it on the Senate calendar.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor action; after placement on the calendar, no vote or debate occurred for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican — 31 of 49 Senate Republicans — and no Democrat or independent supported it; no vote was ever taken.

industries.note: The bill would make union fees voluntary nationwide, cutting the dues unions use to bargain contracts and enforce them. Union strength and the wages of workers who bargain through unions rise and fall together.
With no union security agreements, unions would have fewer resources at the bargaining table, giving employers more leverage over wages and working conditions.
